Equipment: Dumbbell
Mechanics Type: Compound
Level: Beginner

========================================­=====

| Directions |
1. Stand with your feet slightly wider than hip-width apart, holding a pair of light dumbbells down by your sides. Clean the dumbbells up to your shoulders so that one end of each dumbbell rests on top of each shoulder. Balance the dumbbells on your shoulder by holding on to dumbbells with elbows facing forward. This will be your starting position.

2. Keeping your head facing forward, your back straight, and your chest high, squat down by bending your hips back while allowing knees to come forward slightly, keeping your back straight and knees pointed in the same direction as your feet. Descend until your thighs are at parallel, or just past parallel to floor.

3. To return to the starting position, extend your knees and hips until your legs are straight. Repeat for the recommended number of reps.

candidates.title: How to do Dumbbell Front Squats!
How To Properly Do A Dumbbell Front Squat - Movement Standards
candidates.description:
The Dumbbell Front Squat is an effective exercise that targets the lower body, emphasizing the quads, glutes, and hamstrings, while also engaging the core and upper back to maintain posture with the weights in the front rack position. This variation of the traditional squat adds an extra challenge by requiring you to stabilize the load with your upper body. Here’s how to perform a Dumbbell Front Squat correctly:

Setup:
  - Choose a pair of dumbbells that are heavy enough to provide a good workout but not so heavy that you can’t maintain form. Start with lighter weights if you are new to this exercise.
  - Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart or slightly wider, toes pointed slightly outward.

Grip and Position:
  - Clean the dumbbells up to the front rack position. Hold the dumbbells so that one end of each dumbbell rests on each shoulder, or hold them vertically with your elbows pointing forward. Your hands should be in front of your shoulders, supporting the weight.
  - Keep your elbows up throughout the exercise. This helps to stabilize the dumbbells and maintain a good posture.

Execution:
  - Take a deep breath and brace your core. Keep your chest up and your back straight.
  - Begin by pushing your hips back and bending your knees to lower your body into a squat. Make sure to keep the weight in your heels, not your toes.
  - Lower yourself until your thighs are at least parallel to the ground, or go deeper if your mobility allows.

Bottom Position:
  - In the bottom position, pause briefly while maintaining the dumbbells in their stable position and keeping your elbows high.
  - Ensure your knees are in line with your toes and not caving inward.

Ascending Phase:
  - Drive through your heels to push back up to the starting position. Exhale as you ascend.
  - Focus on keeping the dumbbells stable and maintaining an upright torso throughout the movement.

Finish & Repeat:
  - Stand up fully at the top, squeezing your glutes at the end of the movement.
  - Perform the desired number of repetitions, maintaining form and control throughout each rep.

Tips:
  - It’s crucial to keep the elbows up and pointed forward throughout the squat to prevent the dumbbells from shifting and to help maintain balance.
  - If you find it difficult to keep your balance or maintain form, reduce the weight of the dumbbells or practice the movement without weights until you improve your technique.
  - Incorporate pauses at the bottom of the squat to increase the difficulty and enhance muscle engagement.

candidates.title: How To Front Squat (WAYS TO KEEP YOUR CHEST UP!)
candidates.description:
A proper front squat requires you keep your chest upright. Today Dr. Aaron Horschig breaks down the 2 common faults that push your chest forward and kill your performance during the front squat.

1) Limited Ankle Mobility
2) Poor Core Stability 

Get my book on fixing injury here: 
https://www.amazon.com/Rebuilding-Milo-Foundation-Enhancing-Performance/dp/1628604220

Get my book 'The Squat Bible' here: 
https://www.amazon.com/Squat-Bible-Ultimate-Mastering-Strength/dp/1540395421/

Get my 13-Week Squat Program? https://marketplace.trainheroic.com/workout-plan/program/thomas-program-1641592726

Get olympic weightlifting programming (part 1): 
https://marketplace.trainheroic.com/workout-plan/program/vaughn-program-1626381817?attrib=547878-aff-squatu

Get olympic weightlifting programming (part 2): https://marketplace.trainheroic.com/workout-plan/program/vaughn-program-1627319357?attrib=547878-aff-squatu

_________________________________

In order to keep your chest upright and sink into a deep front squat your knees must be able to travel forward towards, or even past your toes. This will allow your body to stay balanced in the deep position. If your knees are unable to move forward as you descend due to limited ankle mobility, your chest will have to collapse forward as compensation. 

However, if you are able to get into a good bottom position but your chest still collapses on the ascent, we can assume the problem is more so due to poor stability. This is because the mobility demands for the front squat are highest in the bottom position. The zombie no hands front squat is one of my favorite training tools to improve your stability in a very movement specific manner. 

If you need help with the needed ankle mobility to perform a full pistol, check out this video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IikP_teeLkI

candidates.title: The Dumbbell Front Squat
candidates.description:
The dumbbell front squat builds on the mechanics of the barbell front squat. The dumbbells may not be supported entirely on the torso as they are with the barbell, but the goal remains the same — to support the load primarily on the shoulders with the elbows pointed forward. Controlling both dumbbells demands and improves midline stability, control, and accurate positioning of the body.
